name: c-kermit
desc: Scriptable network and serial communication for UNIX and VMS
why: Kermit is a fossil of serial and modem communication with a scripting language, though it is deprecated here.

brief.what_it_is: C-Kermit is a command-line communications program for UNIX-family systems (Linux, macOS, BSD, Android and others) and OpenVMS. It opens serial-port, dialed-modem, TCP/IP Telnet, SSH and SSL/TLS connections, runs interactive terminal sessions, transfers files using the Kermit protocol, converts character sets, and automates all of this with a built-in scripting language. Input is typed commands or Kermit script files; output is a live terminal session, transferred files, and script results. The stable release is 9.0.302 from 2011, and C-Kermit 10.0 is in beta testing.
brief.why_it_exists: The project is framed as a single portable package for both network and serial communications, offering automation, helpfulness and language features that the author says are not found in most of the other packages. The homepage describes Kermit as 'a robust and portable platform-and-transport-independent file-transfer protocol' that has run since 1981.
brief.how_it_works: The program is a single C binary that picks one transport (serial, modem, Telnet, SSH) and then runs the same terminal, file-transfer and scripting features over it. Its scripting language, the Kermit script language, automates dialogs and file management. The 9.0 page says its SSH and SSL/TLS clients are built in for the 10.0 beta, and that it can be configured as an SSH subsystem, which fits the kermit-sshsub executable.

brief.install_notes: Brew is not the only route: the project's own page describes building from source. On Unix, run the makefile target matching your OS and then make install, and the makefile includes its own installation procedure. Prebuilt binaries come from an archive frozen in July 2011, and the page advises building your own. For dial-out from Unix, the binary may need a particular owner and group and setuid/setgid bits to reach the serial device and lockfile directory, as with cu or minicom; the installation guide's sections 10 and 11 cover this. The brew package installs ckermit.ini, kermit and kermit-sshsub. I did not verify the ckermit.ini config step in the pages I read.
brief.standout: It combines serial, modem, Telnet and SSH connections, file transfer and a full scripting language in one portable binary, and its own README-equivalent describes it as a replacement for a long list of separate tools such as cu, tip, minicom, telnet, ssh, expect and wget. The Kermit protocol is also decades old and older than most modern terminal tools.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage was updated 15 February 2025 and 24 March 2025, and it lists C-Kermit 10.0 Beta.12 dated 22 March 2025 as the current item. The last stable release is 9.0.302 from 20 August 2011. The scout note calling it 'deprecated' is not supported by the homepage, which describes active beta development.
brief.caveats: The stable 9.0.302 release is from 2011 and the prebuilt binary archive was frozen in July 2011, so for current use the 10.0 beta is the active line. The 9.0 page says the 10.0 beta covers Unix and VMS, with Windows support being Kermit 95, a separate program. The C-Kermit manual is the 2nd edition of the Digital Press book, current with version 6.0. Several older FTP download links are broken in modern browsers, and the project says to use HTTPS or its built-in FTP client. Dial-out permissions can need manual setup. The 9.0 page's build commands may differ for 10.0.
quotes: Portable OPEN SOURCE Scriptable Network and Serial Communication Software for Unix and VMS

C-Kermit can be thought of as a user-friendly and powerful alternative to cu, tip, minicom, uucp, ftp, ftpd, telnet, ktelnet, rlogin, ssh, find, grep, iconv, recode, expect, wget, sendpage, bc, and to some extent even Lisp, your shell, and/or Perl
Kermit is a robust and portable platform-and-transport-independent file-transfer protocol and a large collection of software programs that implement it on a wide variety of platforms.
